deckName: KS3 DT · J3 Lesson 2 — First Words in Python (Teacher Deck)

slides.kicker: OUR LADY'S GRAMMAR SCHOOL · DIGITAL TECHNOLOGY
slides.heading: Lesson 2 · First Words in Python
slides.sub: You write your first Python today, and make the computer print exactly the right words — J3 · Lesson 2 of 17
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: coming in, logging in to the computer, then opening the class link from Google Classroom. The lesson opens itself on the Do-Now, which is a short warm-up of questions from Lesson 1. It marks itself as they settle, and it is never graded and never public.

SAY: "Log in, open the class link, and work through the warm-up questions. When the warm-up hands over to today's card, stop there and look up."

WATCH FOR: a pupil who has not finished Lesson 1 gets no warm-up at all, because it only ever serves questions from lessons that pupil has completed. That screen goes straight to today's card, and it is correct rather than broken.

WHEN TO MOVE: when most of the room is sitting on today's card, stop the room — eyes front.

slides.heading: In this lesson you will…
bullets: Write a line of Python that prints exactly the words you want, and no other words.
Put a word into a box with a name on it, use that box in more than one place, and change it in one place only.
Get Python to work out a sum inside a printed line, then read the console — the strip where a program's words come out — to check the answer.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: eyes front, today's card waiting on their screens.

SAY: "Three things today." Then read the three lines out.

WATCH FOR: the second line is the one that matters most. Typing a name once and printing it twice is the idea the rest of programming stands on, and it is the first time these pupils meet it.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: What a call sheet is
bullets: A call sheet is the single piece of paper a film or theatre crew works from.
It carries the title, the times and the numbers everyone needs for the day, and somebody prints it every morning.
In this Studio the call sheet is printed by a program, and this hour you write that program.
The language is Python. You type it, it is one of the most used languages in the world, and a great deal of real software is written in it.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: eyes front, screens ignored.

SAY: read the four lines out. The pupils' own card says the same thing in their own words in a moment, so they meet it twice on purpose.

THE THING TO KNOW BEFORE YOU START, and it is worth saying to the room in your own words: this class starts Python from zero by design — nothing from last year is assumed. Everything a pupil meets in this hour is taught in this hour. No pupil is behind at the start of it.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: How the hour works
bullets: The job is always the same, and it is the whole lesson: MAKE THE CONSOLE SAY IT.
First a short film, with no sound. Every word you need is written on the screen.
Then four BUILDS. A build is one small job, and each one shows you the exact lines the call sheet must have.
You put the Python together, press RUN, and the console shows you what your program really printed.
Exactly what was asked for gets you MATCHED. Anything else gets you NOT YET, and a run that does not work costs you nothing.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: eyes front. This is the slide that sets the tone for the whole hour.

SAY: read the five lines out, and land the last one hardest. A wrong run is not a mistake to be embarrassed about — it is how the hour is designed to be worked.

WHY: pupils who believe a wrong run costs them something stop pressing RUN and start asking an adult instead, and the adult is not the one who is meant to be checking.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: Ready? Go.
bullets: Back to your screens. Today's card types itself out, so wait for the last line.
We read it together. It tells you what a call sheet is and what this hour asks of you.
Then press Start the film, and watch the film on your own computer.
The film has no sound and it comes in four parts. The buttons underneath jump to any part.
When the film ends, stop and look up.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: about to read today's card on their own screens.

SAY: "Back to your screens. The card types itself out, so wait for the last line before we read it." Wait until the room is on the card before you say another word.

THEN SAY: "We are reading this together." Read it aloud while pupils follow on their own screens. It repeats what you have just said from the front, in the pupils' own words, and it names the four builds in order.

THEN SAY: "Press Start the film. Watch it on your own computer."

WATCH FOR: if the class link is not on Google Classroom, put the QR code from the Classes tab on the board instead.

WHEN TO MOVE: send them into the film, then put the film slide up while they watch.

slides.heading: The film — on your own screen
bullets: The film has no sound, so every word you need is written on the screen. Read as you watch.
It comes in four parts, and the buttons underneath jump to any of them.
The parts are: what Python is · print, exactly · a box with a name on it · reading an error without fear.
If the film will not play, carry on and tell whoever is in the room. Every idea in it is written again on the build cards.
When it ends, stop and look up.
slides.notes:
[FILM — pupil-led: every pupil watches it on their own computer, at their own pace. Nothing is played from the front, and there is nothing here for you to demonstrate.]

WHERE THE CLASS IS: today's card read, the film screen open on every monitor.

SAY: "The film is silent, so read as you watch. It comes in four parts, and the buttons underneath let you go back over any part. When it ends, stop and look up."

WHY IT MATTERS: the film is where a box with a name on it is first shown, and where an error is shown as something to read rather than something to be afraid of. Both come straight back in the builds.

WHILE THEY WATCH: walk the room. Anyone whose film will not play should simply carry on — the build cards carry every idea in it, and the pupil's own screen says so.

WHEN TO MOVE: when most of the room has reached the end of the film, stop everybody for the first two builds.

sections.label: STOP · The top of the call sheet

slides.heading: STOP — eyes front · The top of the call sheet
bullets: Two builds now, and they are the two smallest things Python can do for you.
Print one exact line. Then print two lines, and get them the right way round.
The target at the top of the card is exactly what the console has to print — every letter, every space.
Exact matters here. A capital letter in the wrong place is a different line to the console.
Nothing is taken off you for a run that does not work, and you can run as many times as you like.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: film finished, screens ignored, eyes front. Nobody has written a line of Python yet.

SAY: read the five lines out. The word to lean on is EXACT — the console prints what the program really says, not what the pupil hoped it would say. The card puts it well: it does not guess what you meant, and tonight's audience is standing outside a theatre whose name has to be right.

SAY THIS TOO, because it is what keeps a first coding lesson calm: a wrong run costs a pupil nothing and is part of the design. The lines come straight back and the pupil tries again.

FOR YOU, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS HOUR IS SAFE TO COVER: the checker, not the teacher, is the authority on whether code is correct — you never need to read Python. RUN really runs the pupil's own program, the console shows what it printed, and the card gives the verdict on its own. Your job is the room, not the code.

AND REMEMBER: this class starts Python from zero by design — nothing from last year is assumed. A pupil who says she has never done any of this before is exactly right, and is not behind.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on to the next slide, then send them in.

slides.heading: What a build looks like
bullets: Press Open the call sheet, and the first build opens.
The lines you can use sit under The lines. Drag the ones you want into Your program, in the order you want them to run.
Some lines have a gap in them for you to type into, and each gap says what it wants.
Press RUN my program. The console underneath shows exactly what your program printed.
MATCHED means the console said exactly what the target shows. NOT YET means it did not, and you get the lines back to try again.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: about to open the first build.

SAY: "Press Open the call sheet. Build one is one line long. Build two is two lines, and getting them the right way round is the whole of it."

THEN SAY: "RUN stays asleep until you have moved at least one line into Your program, and the card tells you so."

WHAT THE CONSOLE DOES: it shows what the program really printed. If Python stops instead, it shows Python's own words first and a plain-English line underneath them. The verdict never tells a pupil which line to change — that part is deliberately hers.

IF A GAP IS LEFT EMPTY: RUN does not run at all. The card says which gap is still empty and puts the cursor in it, so nothing fails silently.

WHILE THEY WORK: circulate, and read the CONSOLE over shoulders rather than the verdict. What actually came out tells you what a pupil thinks a line does, which is the only thing worth teaching into.

WHEN TO MOVE: the badge card First Words lands when both builds have matched. When those cards start appearing around the room, stop everybody.

sections.label: STOP · The rest of the call sheet

slides.heading: STOP — eyes front · The rest of the call sheet
bullets: Two more builds, and the first of them is the important one.
So far every word you printed was typed into the line that printed it.
Now the theatre's name goes into a VARIABLE instead: a box with a name on it, holding one value.
Two different lines then use that box. Change what is in the box, and both lines change with it.
Then a sum. Python works it out inside the printed line, so nobody types the answer in.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: the first badge earned, screens ignored, eyes front.

SAY: read the five lines out, and take the middle three slowly. The pupils type the name once, into the gap in the first line, and it comes out twice.

THE PAYOFF, worth saying in your own words: if the show moved to a different theatre tomorrow, you would change one box, and every line that uses it would change with it. That is why anybody bothers with a variable at all.

THE ONE DIFFERENCE BUILD 3 IS REALLY ABOUT: a name used WITHOUT speech marks means the box. The same word INSIDE speech marks is just those letters. The card says it and the film showed it.

DO NOT stand over a pupil reading her Python and correcting it. The checker, not the teacher, is the authority on whether code is correct, and you never need to read Python to help here. Ask what came out in the console instead, and let the pupil tell you.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on to the next slide, then send them in.

slides.heading: What changes in these two builds
bullets: A line with = in it makes a variable: the name on the left, the value on the right.
In Python, = means put this into that box. It does not mean is the same as.
A line that fills a box has to come above any line that uses it.
In the last build, one gap asks what a seat costs and the other asks how many seats there are.
Press RUN, read the console, and fix what needs fixing. Nothing is taken off you for a run that does not work.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: about to open build 3.

SAY: "Press Open the call sheet again. Build three uses one box in two lines. Build four asks Python to do the sum for you."

THEN SAY: "When a build matches, press Next build. After the last one, press Continue."

WHAT THE LAST BUILD ADDS: a number has to be turned into text before it can be joined to words, and the card says exactly how. Python refuses to join a word to a number on its own, and when it refuses the console explains why in plain English underneath Python's own message.

THIS IS THE LONGEST STRETCH OF THE HOUR, so keep circulating. The pupils who need you are the ones whose console still says nothing has run yet.

WHEN TO MOVE: the badge card Call Sheet Printed lands when both builds have matched. When most of the room has it, bring them back together.

sections.label: What you did, and what is next

slides.heading: What you did, and what is next
bullets: Two cards to read on your own, then the last two screens.
The first card names what you now have: a title, two lines in the right order, a name you only had to type once, and a sum the program works out for itself.
Nearly every program you will ever write uses those same four things.
The second card is about next fortnight, when you build a playlist engine.
Every box you made today holds ONE value. A playlist is a list of many, in an order.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: both badges earned, reading two short cards on their own.

SAY: "Two cards, on your own. Read the first one properly — it is the whole of today in four lines."

WHAT THE FIRST CARD DOES: it names the four things the pupils have just used, in the pupils' own words. Those four lines are the ones worth being able to say out loud, and next lesson is built on them.

WHAT THE SECOND CARD SAYS: next fortnight is a playlist engine. There is nothing to bring and nothing to do in between, and this lesson stays open on the year map for anyone who wants to look back through the four builds.

WHEN TO MOVE: when both cards are confirmed, put the next slide up.

slides.heading: One question before you finish
bullets: One question now, on your own, and this one IS marked.
It is about the Python you wrote today, so think about it before you click.
You find out whether you were right, and why, at the very end of the lesson.
That comes after the How did it go? screen, so do not sit waiting for an answer.
slides.notes:
NOTHING ABOUT THE MARKED QUESTION GOES ON THE BOARD. This slide is written so that it cannot answer it, and no other slide in the deck carries the question or any part of it.

WHERE THE CLASS IS: one question, on their own.

SAY: "One question, on your own, and this one is marked. I can see how the class did on it, so no conferring."

THEN SAY: "You find out whether you were right, and why, right at the end — after the last screen. Do not sit waiting for it."

WHY THE VERDICT IS HELD BACK: so that nobody can work out from it whether to change anything on the way through. Tell the class that plainly, or the wait reads as the website being broken.

DO NOT answer it at a desk. It is the one marked thing in the hour, and it is the one honest read you get on the class.

WHEN TO MOVE: when the room has answered, straight on to the last screen.

slides.heading: Before you leave
bullets: How did it go? — three sentences to rate, and one choice about how hard the hour felt.
The comment box goes to your teacher and nobody else. Everyone finishes this screen before leaving.
Sign out every time. If you stay signed in, anything the next person does on this computer looks like you did it.
Chair in, area tidy, nothing left beside your machine.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: on the last screen, then packing up.

SAY: "Last screen. Three sentences to rate, one choice about how hard the hour felt, and a comment box that comes to me and nobody else."

NOBODY LEAVES WITHOUT FINISHING How did it go? It is compulsory, and it is how you hear from the pupils who never put a hand up. After a first hour of real code it matters more than usual: a pupil who found it hard will often say so here and nowhere else.

THEN SAY: "Sign out. Chair in. Nothing left beside your machine."

WHY: the sign-out rule is one the class judged other people against in Lesson 1, so hold them to it here.

WHEN TO MOVE: dismiss when the room is signed out and tidy.
